title: He Filed 64 Identical Asylum Claims for Indian Clients. ICE Just Made Him the First Attorney It's Ever Fined for It.
excerpt: California-based Vinod Doddamani faces a $255,000 penalty in a first-of-its-kind crackdown on immigration attorneys. For the Indian diaspora, the fallout goes far beyond one case.
body:
An Indian-American immigration attorney in California is facing fines exceeding $255,000 after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement accused him of filing dozens of fraudulent asylum applications on behalf of Indian nationals — a first-of-its-kind enforcement action that immigration lawyers across the country are watching closely.

Vinod Doddamani, who operates a nationwide practice primarily representing Indian clients, allegedly submitted 64 fraudulent documents across 32 immigration cases, according to the Department of Homeland Security's investigative arm, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI). The agency issued five separate notices of intent to fine Doddamani, making this the first time ICE has pursued financial penalties against an attorney for filing false asylum claims.

## What the Government Found

The allegations centre on a pattern DHS describes as strikingly uniform. Doddamani's asylum applications for Indian clients reportedly contained "identical or nearly identical" language and factual narratives regarding persecution claims. In short, the government is saying dozens of supposedly unique asylum seekers told virtually the same story, word for word.

"The days of attorneys abusing and defrauding our immigration system are over," ICE said in a public statement posted on X (formerly Twitter).

The case follows a directive issued in May by DHS General Counsel James Percival, who instructed ICE attorneys to pursue enforcement actions against immigration lawyers caught filing false claims. Prior to this directive, DHS had never attempted to fine or penalise attorneys for fraudulent asylum filings — making the Doddamani case a precedent-setting move.



> **""The days of attorneys abusing and defrauding our immigration system are over," ICE said in a public statement posted on X (formerly Twitter)."**


> "Fraudulent asylum applications pose a risk to public safety by overburdening the immigration system and hindering the expulsion of dangerous individuals."
> — James Percival, DHS General Counsel

## Why This Hits the Diaspora Differently

For the hundreds of thousands of Indians navigating the U.S. immigration system — whether on H-1B work visas, student F-1s, or asylum claims — the case raises uncomfortable questions. Fraudulent filings by a handful of attorneys don't just hurt the individuals involved. They provide ammunition to those who argue the system is being gamed, making it harder for legitimate applicants.

Indian nationals already face some of the longest green card backlogs in the world, with employment-based wait times stretching into decades. The community has been under heightened scrutiny since the Trump administration's return to aggressive immigration enforcement, including the proposed $100,000 H-1B fee hike, tighter student visa rules, and a crackdown on "Day 1 CPT" programmes that thousands of Indian professionals use as a bridge while waiting for H-1B lottery results.

The Doddamani case isn't about H-1B holders or skilled workers — it's about asylum seekers. But the ripple effect is real. Every headline about immigration fraud involving Indian nationals feeds a narrative that can shape policy.

## A Growing Crackdown

This case is not isolated. The Trump administration has been methodically expanding its immigration enforcement toolkit. In a separate action last week, DHS fined an attorney over $255,000 — the same amount at stake in the Doddamani case — for filing fraudulent claims. Federal Trade Commission data show at least 920 immigration service scams were reported in 2025, more than the first three years of the Biden administration combined.

The DOJ has also recently filed denaturalisation actions against 17 individuals, including Indian-born Neeraj Sharma of Magnavision LLC, a New Jersey staffing company accused of filing 11 fraudulent H-1B petitions with forged corporate letters and signatures.

## What Happens Next

Doddamani has not yet been criminally charged — the current action is civil. The $255,000 fine is based on the five notices of intent, and he will have the opportunity to contest them. But the signal from Washington is unmistakable: the era of lenient enforcement against immigration attorneys is over.

For Indian families navigating the system — whether they're waiting on green cards, renewing H-1Bs, or filing legitimate asylum claims — the message is to be extremely careful about who represents them. A fraudulent filing doesn't just risk deportation. It can permanently bar re-entry to the United States.

*Sources: Fox News, News Dive, Department of Justice, Department of Homeland Security*
